question: Will the Ohio Supreme Court dispose of the appeal in Borovicanin v. NCAA (No. 2026-1353) on the merits by October 30, 2026?

calls.reasoning: Status quo is NO: as of the Oct 19 daily archive only procedural/stay orders exist in 2026-1353. Ohio Supreme Court discretionary-appeal jurisdiction decisions typically take months; with a stay already protecting the players there is little urgency to issue a merits disposition within 11 days of supplemental briefs. Mootness via DeWine's EO is partial at best (plaintiffs include out-of-state players at Gonzaga/St. John's; EO is under federal challenge), and a moot dismissal would dissolve the stay. Upside: the court explicitly asked about mootness, has moved very fast (prior related matter dismissed Sept 28), and the season opens early November; settlement/voluntary dismissal also counts. No human market found (Polymarket/Manifold/Kalshi none).

Mootness via the DeWine order is weak: plaintiffs at out-of-state schools (Gonzaga's Bennett, St. John's Hall) aren't covered and the order doesn't bind the NCAA. Declining jurisdiction days after granting a stay would be self-contradictory, and accepting jurisdiction plus ruling within ~10 days is implausible under normal Practice Rule timing. Upside risk: this court moves fast (the related case 2026-1245 was dismissed about two weeks after its emergency motion), and the parties could settle or dismiss. calls.reconciliation: All three runs agree on the facts: only procedural/stay orders (Oct 6, Oct 14) in 2026-1353 through Oct 19; mootness briefs due Oct 19; EO is permissive and Ohio-only; NCAA's federal suit filed Oct 16; related case 2026-1245 dismissed Sept 28; no market. The 0.09 vs 0.14 split is pure judgment about how much the court's speed and its mootness inquiry should count. I weigh the stay pending appeal, the weak mootness case, and normal jurisdiction timing most heavily, and keep some weight on a fast dismissal or settlement. Landing at 0.12 reflects that weighing.
